reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / KDIGO glomerular disease guidance
clinicalPearls: Caused by cold-precipitable immunoglobulins that deposit in small vessels and drive immune-complex vasculitis
Mixed (type II and III) cryoglobulinaemia is strongly linked to chronic hepatitis C virus infection, which should be tested for in every case
The classic Meltzer triad is palpable purpura, arthralgia, and weakness, typically affecting dependent areas of the legs
Peripheral neuropathy, often a painful sensory or sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis are important organ manifestations
Serum complement typically shows a low C4 out of proportion to C3, and rheumatoid factor is frequently positive
Type I cryoglobulinaemia is monoclonal and associated with lymphoproliferative or plasma cell disorders, more often causing hyperviscosity and digital ischaemia

Treatment targets the underlying cause, with direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis-C-driven disease and immunosuppression such as rituximab and glucocorticoids for severe organ-threatening vasculitis
reference.pathophysiology: Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that reversibly precipitate at temperatures below core body temperature and redissolve on warming. In mixed cryoglobulinaemia a polyclonal or monoclonal immunoglobulin with rheumatoid-factor activity binds polyclonal IgG, forming immune complexes that deposit in small and medium vessels, activate complement, and trigger a leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Chronic hepatitis C virus infection is the dominant driver, providing sustained antigenic stimulation that expands rheumatoid-factor-producing B-cell clones. Vascular deposition produces cutaneous purpura, immune-complex glomerulonephritis (often membranoproliferative), and vasa nervorum involvement causing neuropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia or other lymphoproliferative disease
Septic or embolic causes of purpura
additionalInvestigations: Serum cryoglobulin assay with correct warm collection and transport technique
Hepatitis C (and hepatitis B, HIV) serology and viral load
Complement levels showing characteristically low C4, plus rheumatoid factor
Urinalysis and renal function to detect glomerulonephritis
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to characterise the cryoglobulin type
Skin or renal biopsy demonstrating immune-complex vasculitis or membranoproliferative pattern
redFlags: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with haematuria and rising creatinine
Widespread skin necrosis or digital ischaemia suggesting severe or hyperviscosity-related disease
Progressive motor neuropathy or foot drop
Features of hyperviscosity such as visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding, and confusion in type I disease
Gut or cardiac involvement indicating severe systemic vasculitis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause and organ involvement; hepatitis-C-related disease often improves markedly with viral eradication, whereas severe renal disease, extensive neuropathy, and underlying lymphoproliferative disorders worsen prognosis.
pitfalls: False-negative cryoglobulin results from allowing the sample to cool before separation
Failing to test for hepatitis C in every patient with mixed cryoglobulinaemia
Misreading a low C4 with normal C3 as insignificant rather than a supportive clue
Treating with immunosuppression alone when an underlying infection or clonal disorder needs directed therapy
references: KDIGO clinical practice guidance on glomerular diseases
